big: ₹10,000 a month for 10 years is ₹12 lakh put in. At an assumed 12% a year, the maths gives about ₹23 lakh. Nearly half is growth. But 12% is an assumption, not a promise.

lines: Only if markets deliver the assumed rate. Each instalment compounds from its own date. Treat it as an illustration, never a forecast.

alt: Bars of money put in and the assumed corpus
caps: At an assumed 12%, about ₹23 lakh. Not a forecast.

q: ₹10,000 a month for 10 years at an assumed 12% a year gives about what?
why: ₹12 lakh is only the money put in.
The standard formula gives about ₹23.2 lakh.
₹36 lakh is far above what the formula gives.
₹14 lakh is too low for 12% over 10 years.

q: What is the best way to describe such a result to a client?
opts: A promised outcome for her goals
A guaranteed minimum corpus for her
An illustration on an assumed rate
A forecast made by the fund house
why: No result of this kind can be promised.
Nothing here is a guaranteed minimum.
The rate is an assumption, so it is an illustration.
A fund house does not forecast like this.

q: What usually helps a long-term SIP more than chasing a higher rate?
opts: Starting early and raising it yearly
Waiting for a market fall to come
why: Time and step-ups matter, since you control them.
Frequent switching adds cost and tax. It does not answer what was asked.
Waiting means missing growth. It does not answer what was asked.
Stopping in dips breaks compounding. The details here point elsewhere.

q: Why does an early instalment grow more than a late one?
opts: It is larger in amount paid
It is taxed less than later ones
It is chosen by SEBI itself
It compounds for a longer time
why: All instalments in a plain SIP are equal in amount. It does not answer what was asked.
Tax does not explain the gap between instalments. It does not answer what was asked.
SEBI plays no part in how instalments grow. The details here point elsewhere.
Each instalment compounds from its own date, so earlier ones run longer.

pts: A SIP's instalments each compound from their own date.
The ₹23 lakh figure assumes 12%: an illustration.
Start early and step up: you control these.
